title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: eāmus IS THE SECOND AND LAST SUBJUNCTIVE OF THIS LEVEL, and like M1's velim it is taught as a word rather than as a mood. 'Let us go' — the alternative was the plain future ībimus?, and it was rejected because that asks about fact where this module needs an invitation. Two fixed forms in ten modules, both vocabulary. The productive subjunctive is L3-M4's, and nothing here is a licence to write another.

TIME IS AN ABLATIVE AND TAKES NO PREPOSITION: hōrā sextā, 'at the sixth hour'. L1-M4 taught the caseless time adverbs — cotīdiē, crās, herī — and promised this; here it lands. It is the same ending that follows opus est, that means 'by' in raedā, and that follows in and cum, now doing a fourth job — and the number agrees with the hour, so both words wear the long ā. A Roman hour was a twelfth of the daylight, not sixty minutes.

THE FIRST-PERSON PLURAL -mus OPENS HERE and it is real new person-marking: venīmus, bibimus, legimus, edimus, īmus. L1 wrote -ō, -s and -t, and L1-M10 reached for agimus exactly once. nōs exists and is written ONCE in this module, for stress — the ending already says 'we', and a pronoun in every sentence is the anglophone tell L1-M10 spent a rule on.

mēcum PUTS THE PREPOSITION AFTER THE PRONOUN AND JOINS IT ON: 'with me' is mēcum, never cum mē. It is the only place in L1 or L2 where cum behaves like that, there is no rule to derive it from, and it is learned as a word. nōbīscum ('with us') does the same and is named here and written nowhere.

AN INVITATION USES L1-M2's QUESTION MACHINERY UNCHANGED: venīs-ne mēcum? The -ne rides on the host verb, which L1-M9 already taught, so nothing new is being built — and an invitation is accepted by repeating its verb (ita, veniō), because Latin has no bare yes. quandō is already a question word and takes no -ne: two question marks on one sentence is L1-M2's rule coming back.

words.note: 'Let us go' — a subjunctive, which is a mood this course does not explain yet. Take it whole, as the word that turns going into an invitation. M1's velim is the only other one.
'Home', with no preposition — M4's word, and going home needs nothing in front of it.

sentences.trap: One word does what English needs three for. eāmus is not 'we go' and not 'we will go' — it is a suggestion, and Latin marks that with a mood rather than with words around the verb. This is the second and last such form in the level.
sentences.sound: E-ā-mus DO-mum. Three syllables and a long ā in the middle: the invitation is in that vowel.

M1's quaesō, softening a suggestion rather than an order
a plain statement instead of a suggestion

mistake.why: the plain 'we go' used for a suggestion. It is correct Latin and it says something else: it reports what is happening rather than proposing it, and an invitation that reports is not an invitation.

words.note: 'When', asking a question. It is not one of M4's qu- words by accident — quandō, quō, quod, quid, quālis and quantus are all one family, and only the vowels part them.
'Let us go' — a subjunctive taken whole. In a question it asks for a decision rather than making one.

sentences.trap: A suggestion and a question at once, and no -ne anywhere. quandō is already a question word, so the particle would be a second question mark on the same sentence — L1-M2's rule, coming back on a new word.

variations.changed: asked of one person about a fact
the new -mus ending on a different verb
the same ending on the verb of coming

sentences.cue: We come at the sixth hour.

words.note: 'At the hour' — the ablative, which is how Latin says WHEN. No preposition: the ending alone means 'at'. L1-M4 promised this and wrote it nowhere.
'Sixth', agreeing with hōrā and so wearing the same ending. L1-M8's numbers counted things; this one places them in the day.
'I come': veniō 'I come', venīs 'you come', venit 'he comes', venīmus 'we come'. The -mus is the new one, and it is the ending that means 'we'.

sentences.trap: Three things at once: a case doing 'at', an adjective agreeing inside it, and the new -mus. The ablative here is M4's ending doing a third job — after opus est, as a means, and now as a time — and every one of them works by the ending alone.
sentences.sound: HŌ-rā SEX-tā ve-NĪ-mus. Two long ā endings that rhyme, exactly as L2-M3 said agreement sounds.

mistake.why: 'in' borrowed from English 'at six'. The ending is already the 'at', exactly as it was already the 'by' in raedā — and this is the second time in three modules that an English preposition tries to attach itself to a case that does not need one.

sentences.mnemonic: The hour wears the same ending as its number.

words.note: 'I come': veniō 'I come', venīs 'you come', venit 'he comes', venīmus 'we come'. The -mus is the new one, and it is the ending that means 'we'.
The question mark, written as an ending: it rides on the back of the first word and turns a statement into a yes/no question. L1-M2's particle, and the hyphen is this course's.
'With me' — one word, with the preposition AFTER the pronoun. cum mē is wrong; mēcum is the form, and it is the only place in this course where cum sits behind its word.

sentences.trap: cum goes backwards and joins on. Everywhere else in the course a preposition comes first — ad scholam, in scholā, cum magistrō — and with a pronoun it flips and fuses. There is no rule to derive it from; mēcum is a word.

mistake.why: cum put in front, on the model of every other preposition in the course. It is the most reasonable mistake in the module and it is still wrong — and nōbīscum ('with us') does the same thing, which this course names and does not write.

sentences.mnemonic: With a pronoun, cum rides behind.

words.note: 'We' — and you will almost never need it, because bibimus already says 'we'. Writing it puts the stress on who, exactly as L1-M10 said of ego.
'Wine', and it is neuter: vīnum is the subject shape and the object shape both. M5's word.
'We drink' — bibō 'I drink', bibis 'you drink', bibit 'he drinks', bibimus 'we drink'. L1-M5's verb with the new ending.

sentences.trap: nōs is in this sentence to be noticed. The ending carries 'we' on its own, so the pronoun adds emphasis and nothing else — and it is the ONE sentence in this module that writes it, because a 'we' in every line is the anglophone tell L1-M10 spent a rule on.

variations.changed: nōs dropped, which is the ordinary way to say it

sentences.usage: Said when someone has just said what THEY are drinking.

words.note: 'Book' as the object: liber as the subject, librum as the thing read. L1-M4's word.
'We read' — legō 'I read', legis 'you read', legit 'he reads', legimus 'we read'. L1-M4's verb with the new ending.

sentences.trap: Two words, and one of them is doing the work of three English ones. No pronoun and no auxiliary: legimus is 'we are reading', and everything about who and how many is in the last three letters.

words.note: 'When', asking a question — the sixth qu- word in the course and the only one that asks about time.
'Dinner' — cēna as the subject, cēnam as the thing eaten. M5's word, and the one meal a Roman day had.
'We eat' — edō's plural, and one of the shapes that collides with nothing. edō, edis, ēst, ēs, edere, edimus: six shapes of one verb and two of them are traps.

sentences.trap: edimus is the safe shape of a dangerous verb. ēst is one bar from 'he is' and ēs one from 'you are', and the plural is clear of both — which is worth knowing, because it means the 'we' form is the one you can say without watching your vowels.

sentences.cue: Let's go at the third hour.

words.note: 'At the hour' — the ablative, which is how Latin says WHEN. No preposition: the ending alone means 'at'. L1-M4 promised this and wrote it nowhere.
'Third', agreeing with hōrā. A Roman hour was a twelfth of the daylight, so the third hour is mid-morning rather than three o'clock.
'Let us go' — the subjunctive taken whole, and it takes a time as happily as a destination.

sentences.trap: The suggestion and the time in one line, and neither needs a word to hold it up: no 'shall' and no 'at'. A Roman hour is also not our hour — it stretched in summer and shrank in winter, because it was a twelfth of the daylight rather than sixty minutes.

words.note: 'Yes' — literally 'so'. L1-M2's word, and Latin's nearest thing to a bare yes: it agrees with whatever was just asked.
'I come': veniō 'I come', venīs 'you come', venit 'he comes', venīmus 'we come'. The -mus is the new one, and it is the ending that means 'we'.

sentences.trap: The answer repeats the verb. Latin has no word that means yes on its own account — ita says 'so it is', and repeating the verb of the question is the commonest way to agree. So an invitation is accepted with the verb it was made with.

variations.cue: Yes, you are coming with me.

sentences.cue: We are going home at the sixth hour.

words.note: 'Home', with no preposition — M4's word, and it is the destination shape.
'At the hour' — the ablative, which is how Latin says WHEN. No preposition: the ending alone means 'at'. L1-M4 promised this and wrote it nowhere.
'Sixth', agreeing with hōrā and wearing its ending. The sixth hour was the middle of the day, so this is around noon.
'I go': eō 'I go', īs 'you go', it 'he goes', īmus 'we go'. Four shapes of one very short verb, and only the ending tells you who.

sentences.trap: Four words and three of them refuse a preposition: domum needs none, hōrā needs none, and the verb needs no pronoun. This is what a Latin sentence looks like when every ending is pulling its weight, and English would use five extra words to say it.
sentences.sound: DO-mum HŌ-rā SEX-tā Ī-mus. Short, long, long, long — the whole back half of the line is heavy.

mistake.display: Ad domum in hōrā sextā īmus.
mistake.why: both prepositions put back, because English has both. Each one on its own is the module's mistake; together they are what a sentence looks like when a learner has stopped trusting the endings.
